questions.q: What are the six stages of the software delivery lifecycle covered in this lesson?
options: Plan, code, build, test, release, deploy/operate
Design, develop, debug, document, deliver, delete
Sprint, standup, retro, demo, release, party
Code, commit, push, pull, merge, close
questions.explain: The six stages are plan, code, build, test, release, and deploy/operate — the full path a change takes from idea to running in production.

questions.q: Which stages does CI/CD primarily automate?
options: Plan and Code
Build, Test, Release, and Deploy
Only Deploy
All six stages equally, including Plan
questions.explain: CI/CD automates the build, test, release, and deploy stages — the manual, repetitive work between a finished pull request and code running in production. Plan and Code remain human-driven.

questions.q: In the Northbridge Retail 'save for later' example, what happens at the Build stage?
options: The product manager writes the spec
Merging the pull request triggers a pipeline that builds a new container image for the cart service
The feature is deployed directly to customers with no testing
Dashboards show how often shoppers use the button
questions.explain: The Build stage is where merging code triggers the pipeline to compile and package the change — in this case, into a new container image for the cart service.

questions.q: Why do Plan and Code stay fundamentally human stages?
options: Because no tooling exists yet for writing code
Because a pipeline can't decide what a product should do or write the first draft of a feature
Because they are the least important stages
Because only managers are allowed to touch them
questions.explain: Deciding what to build and writing the first version of a feature require human judgment and creativity that pipelines don't provide — that's why CI/CD starts at Build, not Plan.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'Release' from a 'Deploy' in the lifecycle?
options: They are exactly the same thing
A release is a tested, versioned artifact made available to deploy; a deploy is actually making that release run where it can be reached
A release always happens after a deploy
Only Deploy involves automated tests
questions.explain: Release means the artifact is tested, tagged, and available (e.g. pushed to a registry); Deploy means that release is actually running in an environment users or systems can reach.
